extracted.intended_audience: public relations students and practitioners preparing press releases and media materials
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation criteria for preparing, formatting, timing, distributing, and evaluating press/news releases for print and broadcast media. Covers newsworthiness, managerial justification, format checklists, broadcast requirements, embargoes, distribution channels, and follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Associated Press (AP) style and capitalization rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtually every journalism and public relations writing course requires students to use the Associated Press style manual; news releases that follow AP style will please an editor and increase chances of media use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize only proper names and full organizations (e.g., 'Consolidated Edison' but 'Con Ed's rate advisory board' rather than 'Rate Advisory Board'). Use standard AP usage and copyediting marks throughout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate writing for message retention and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the principal objective of writing is message retention, evaluate your writing by letting it sit and then reading to see if you retained the message and understand what you want to say; have someone else read it and tell you what they took away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use readability tests (see Chapter 9) and techniques such as the signaled stopping technique (SST) where readers note why they stop (confusion, rereading, disagreement) to identify rewrite needs. Remember: good writing is rewritten.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have a managerial reason before issuing a release
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases should not be used unless there is a solid management reason for communicating the message; releases are often overused when practitioners use them because they don't know what else to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider which public needs to be exposed to and retain the message and whether mass media are the best channel. Apply the PR model (press-agent, public-information, two-way asymmetric/symmetric) to decide whether and how to use releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness: identify appropriate occasions for releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Use releases for newsworthy events meaningful to target media/audiences, such as management appointments, changes in advertising agency, plant modernization, milestones (anniversaries, millionth customer), cost savings, selection by another institution, awards, research results, contests, or even bad news that must be communicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the event will interest local weeklies, trade journals, business press, or special publics; remember releases can cover both good and bad news (e.g., plant fires).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meet journalistic standards to get on the media agenda
rubrics_metrics.description: To get on the media agenda your release must meet journalistic standards; media gatekeepers select items that fit their news values and agendas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write releases so they are clear, complete, and interesting; craft them to provide tips, ideas, data, or starting points that reporters can use and rewrite in their own style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match content and style to the communication behavior of publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether publics will actively seek or passively process a story depends largely on the medium: general newspapers/radio/TV typically carry low-involvement information while trade publications and specialized magazines attract active information seekers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write straightforward stories for specialized publications (which may find a technical topic interesting regardless of style) and make general-media stories accessible and engaging for low-involvement readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider cost in time and money before issuing a release
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases take staff time and resources (mailing, photocopying, PR wire fees), so consider whether postage or staff time is justified or whether your time could be better spent on another technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use time-budgeting techniques (Gantt charts, PERT, critical-path) to schedule releases and ensure arrival at optimal time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate release effectiveness systematically
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether your communication and message retention objectives have been met by tracking media use and retention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a clipping service or monitor media yourself to see if releases were used; compare used vs. unused releases, ask editors why they didn't use some releases, and periodically employ formal readership and retention studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting and physical presentation checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: A release should be easy for an editor to hand to a rewrite person: print on one side only of plain white mimeo paper; double-spacing is standard; use a standard, clean typewriter face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-quality mimeo preferred; for one-or-two copies crisp photocopies of the typewritten original are acceptable. For radio-only releases consider special large-type machines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heading elements and top-of-page layout
rubrics_metrics.description: The heading across the top (about one-fifth of the page) should be distinctive but uncluttered and usually include: a large single word NEWS, 'For immediate release' (or release date/embargo indication), name/address/phone of contact, and optionally the release date and serial number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include contact info so reporters can get additional information; use serial/dates when generating many releases daily to facilitate reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a clear sample headline
rubrics_metrics.description: A sample headline can summarize the main point and occasionally be used by newspapers; it should be simple, direct, and written in the active voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'WHEELING STEEL APPOINTS LOCKE TO HEAD PITTSVILLE FOUNDRY'. If no headline is provided, leave room for the editor to write one; ease of processing influences whether a marginally newsworthy release gets used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a dateline/ge-line appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Start the story with a ge-line (town name) rather than always including a date; some papers put the dateline in the body while others prefer it at the top.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize local place names selectively (to highlight them for editors who skim) and consider folding/marking releases to make local names jump out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use standard copyediting marks, paging conventions, and slugs
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard newspaper copyediting marks should be used throughout; if the release runs more than one page use 'more' at the bottom of each page except the last and an end sign such as '30' or '#'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slug successive pages at the top (e.g., 'PROMOTIONS—add one', 'PROMOTIONS—add two') using a slug word from the first paragraph to key the most important aspect of the news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcast release format and conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcast releases have different requirements: type entirely in large capital letters, keep to no more than 200 words (≈1 minute), use short paragraphs (often one sentence per paragraph), and display sentence breaks clearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate clauses/long sentences with ellipses (...) to indicate pauses; avoid contractions, hard-to-pronounce words, and abbreviations; provide pronunciation help in parentheses immediately after unfamiliar names (e.g., 'Tomas Arguea (toe-MAS ar-GWAY-ah)').

rubrics_metrics.name: Write broadcast openings to 'index' the story, not to bury facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not put names, figures, or other critical information in the opening phrase or sentence; the first sentence should index the story for the listener and catch attention by naming the general topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong example: 'Deputy Director of Finance Hiram Williams today submitted a $4.2 million budget…' Right example: 'It will cost less to run the city next year. A budget of over four million dollars was…'

rubrics_metrics.name: Make a spokesperson available and prepare them
rubrics_metrics.description: One thing that may sell a release to radio is the availability of a spokesperson willing to be interviewed; indicate availability and phone number on the release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the spokesperson has a copy of the release and an outline of likely interview material; for talk-show appearances attach a brief note summarizing expertise and availability and include your contact number.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing: allow adequate lead time for submission and processing
rubrics_metrics.description: Sufficient lead time must be allowed when submitting a news release—especially when photographs are included; only with advance alerting are you likely to get major play with less than a day lead time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan at least two or three days for mail delivery and two or three additional days for media processing unless using courier; anticipate events with positive PR value and schedule accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use embargoes carefully and only when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: An embargo places a release date on material so the media are expected to hold information until that time; it is used when media must have material in advance (e.g., scholarship winners, conference presentations, speech text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reasonable embargo most media will observe is the 6 a.m. release to reach morning papers and drive-time radio. Avoid arbitrary embargoes; media may ignore or discard embargoed releases if they seem meaningless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hand-deliver sensitive or high-stakes releases
rubrics_metrics.description: When announcements will create clear winners and losers (major personnel changes) or in crisis situations (government charges, accidents with injuries), hand delivery may be necessary to control timing and confidentiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public relations chiefs may personally prepare, safeguard, and hand-deliver releases when appropriate; in crisis, prepare on-site press releases and briefings for immediate distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address and target submissions to the right editor or news director
rubrics_metrics.description: For print media address the release to 'Editor' and for broadcast to 'News Director'; because of volume, target releases to the appropriate desk or specialized editor (business editor, education, women's editor) for better placement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use directories (Editor & Publisher Yearbook, Broadcasting Yearbook) to find names, but be aware listings get out of date; selective mailings and offering exclusives can get better play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide when to be selective vs. blanket in distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: If the release is routine, it may be sent broadly; if you prepare special material (exclusive articles or photos) tailor and alert selected editors by phone to increase interest and perceived exclusivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh benefits: exclusive features can get major play, while routine announcements sent widely keep the organization's name in editors' minds. Provide different photos/shots to competing media to prevent duplication-driven rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include art and photographs to enhance news value
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographs, tables, graphs, or diagrams play an important role in selling a news release; news kits with photos and biographical material increase the chance of use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare photographs and cutlines according to best practices (see Chapter 27); allow extra lead time for the media's art departments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use PR wire services for timely distribution and specialized targeting
rubrics_metrics.description: PR Newswire and regional services electronically transmit releases to many news and business media for a fee, with options to hold for timed transmission and to target all media or specialized publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use PR Newswire’s Investors Research Wire for investor-related news; transmission can be by messenger, Telex, fax, or dictation; wires help meet timely disclosure requirements and overcome postal delays or outdated contact lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider information-retrieval services and archival/publication effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Releases sent via PR Newswire may become part of computer-stored databases (e.g., NEXIS) used by researchers; storage is 'analogous to publication' because even unreprinted releases remain accessible to researchers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that distribution via electronic services gives releases long-term availability and access beyond immediate media pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow up appropriately with 'thank-you' and relationship-building
rubrics_metrics.description: When coverage genuinely benefits your organization, follow up with a call or note of thanks to the journalist to reward and encourage future favorable coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not thank after every little release (you may become a nuisance), but use sincere thanks when warranted to sustain good journalist-PR relations and ethical reciprocity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use press conferences and press events selectively and prepare for risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Press conferences are appropriate when giving press a chance to question experts will improve coverage; press parties are appropriate for milestones or celebrity attendance. But events can fail (weak news, no-show reporters, poor interviewee performance, timing conflicts, or broadcast/print friction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh potential miscues before proceeding; prepare guests, provide adequate briefing materials, and consider logistics, timing, and likely competing news.
